newsitem.title: FRANCE: French carmakers split on incentives strategy.
newsitem.headline: French carmakers split on incentives strategy.

text.p: France's two car companies hold opposing views on what should be done when a government car rebate scheme that has underpinned the market for the past year expires at the end of September.
Their disagreement mirrors a reported clash over the scheme between the French finance and industry ministries.
Car industry officials say the decision lies with Prime Minister Alain Juppe, who is expected to announce it soon.

PSA Peugeot Citroen chairman Jacques Calvet is asking the government either to lower the value added tax on car sales or else introduce rebates proportional to the price of the car purchased, a company spokeswoman said.
"Mr. Calvet does not think the market will rebound naturally," she told Reuters.
The current scheme, which provides rebates of between 5,000 and 7,000 francs for car buyers turning in old clunkers, has spurred demand for cars in a sluggish consumer spending climate.
The French carmakers' association CCFA said more than 30 percent of last month's car sales, which were up 29 percent, were linked to the scheme.

But rival carmaker Renault SA, which marked its entry this summer into the private sector, does not want an extension of the rebate scheme. "We're not seeking any new support measures," said a Renault spokesman.

He said Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer opposed the incentives on the grounds that they skewed sales toward less expensive cars -- with thinner profit margins -- and disrupted the used-car market, causing distortions in re-sale prices.
Industry Minister Franck Borotra spoke in favour of the incentives on Thursday but said no decision had been taken on whether to extend them beyond the scheduled September 30 expiry.
"I've put some proposals to the prime minister and it's up to him to decide," Borotra told the newspaper Les Echos.

Ministry officials declined to elaborate on Borotra's proposals, which appear to put him at odds with Finance Minister Jean Arthuis, reputed to be a longstanding opponent of the scheme who was overruled last year.
One of Arthuis' aides, Christian Noyer, said on Thursday that no new measures to spur spending would be introduced during the 1997 budget planning process.

The rebate incentives were first put in place in 1993 by the previous government of Prime Minister Edouard Balladur to jump-start a recovery in the French car industry, which plunged into recession following its best year ever in 1992.

Car analysts said Balladur's scheme had the effect of inflating the market artificially by pulling sales forward. Their interpretation appeared to be vindicated last summer when sales slumped after the first scheme expired on June 30, 1995.
Juppe's government revived the scheme with a few changes last October with the stated aim of clearing the streets of the oldest and dirtiest cars.
But its true objective appeared to be the preservation of jobs in the industry, one of France's biggest employers.
"I feel that the supports to the car industry...generate more in terms of activity and tax receipts than they cost," Borotra said.

Analysts say the industry faces a repeat of the surge-and-crash sales pattern seen last year when the current scheme expires, but they say the shock would be preferable to the distortions caused by what some call the addictive supports.
